title: Jaipur
insights: The document shows Jaipur as a rapidly expanding metropolis with over three million residents, a sizable municipal budget, and ongoing large‑scale infrastructure projects such as the Dravyavati River rejuvenation. These demographic and service‑capacity details highlight the pressure on transport networks, the need for flood‑resilient corridors, and the importance of integrating future mobility plans with the city’s planned urban development.
key_facts: Jaipur had a population of approximately 3.1 million in the 2011 census, ranking it as the tenth most populous city in India.
An official municipal report lists Jaipur Municipal Corporation's population at 3,046,163 residents and 599,507 households.
The city recorded a sex ratio of 900 females per 1,000 males and a literacy rate of 83.33 % among residents aged seven and above.
Scheduled Castes comprised 12.88 % (392,285 people) and Scheduled Tribes 3.78 % (115,258 people) of Jaipur’s population.

Hindi is the official language, with 69.69 % of the 2011 census respondents reporting it as their mother tongue; other languages include Rajasthani (9.85 %), Urdu (5.86 %), Marwari (4.36 %), Dhundari (3.93 %) and Sindhi (2.54 %).
According to the 2011 census, 77.9 % of Jaipur’s residents identified as Hindu, 18.6 % as Muslim, 2.4 % as Jain and 1.1 % as other religions.
Jaipur covers a total area of 467 square kilometres (180 sq mi) as defined by the Jaipur Municipal Corporation.
The municipal budget for fiscal year 2022–23 was estimated at ₹8,950 lakh (approximately US$9.3 million).
Key revenue sources for the corporation include house tax, urban development tax, octroi compensation, and various fees and user charges.
Jaipur’s fire protection services operate 11 fire stations equipped with 50 fire tenders.
The Jaipur Water Supply and Sewerage Board, established in 2018, manages water supply and sewerage services across four drainage zones.
The city’s sewerage system includes 730 km of sewer lines and a treatment capacity of 442 million litres per day (MLD).

A 13‑km stretch of the Dravyavati Riverfront was opened after rejuvenation in 2018, with the full 47.5‑km project completed in 2022 following a 2015 redevelopment plan by the Jaipur Development Authority.
On 6 July 2019, Jaipur was added to the UNESCO World Heritage Cities list.
In August 1981, heavy rains caused a cloudburst that flooded large parts of the city, including the airport, resulting in eight fatalities and extensive damage to the Dravyavati River.

title: Jaipur district
insights: Jaipur district’s large and rapidly growing population—over 6.6 million in 2011 with a 26.9% decadal increase—combined with a modestly high density of 598 inhabitants/km² and more than half of residents living in urban areas creates strong demand for efficient transport infrastructure. The district’s geography, bounded by the Thar Desert to the east and the Aravalli hills on three sides, constrains corridor alignment, while its linguistic and socio‑economic diversity underscores the need for inclusive, multimodal planning that links dense urban cores with peripheral rural and hill zones.
key_facts: Jaipur district, located in Rajasthan, northern India, has its headquarters in the city of Jaipur, which is also the state capital and the largest city in the state.
The district covers an area of 11,143 square kilometres, representing about 3.26% of Rajasthan’s total area and ranking ninth in size among the state’s districts.
Geographically, Jaipur district lies between 26°23' and 27°51' north latitude and 74°55' and 76°50' east longitude, stretching roughly 180 km east‑west and 110 km north‑south.

The district borders Sikar district and the state of Haryana to the north, Tonk district to the south, Alwar, Dausa and Sawai Madhopur districts to the east, and Nagaur and Ajmer districts to the west.
The eastern edge of the district abuts the Thar Desert, and the Aravalli mountain range surrounds it on three sides, with notable hill ranges such as Puranaghat and Nahargarh within Jaipur tehsil.
According to the 2011 Census, Jaipur district had a population of 6,626,178, making it the tenth most populous district in India out of 640 districts at that time.
The 2011 Census recorded a population density of 598 inhabitants per square kilometre (1,550 per sq mi) in Jaipur district.
Between 2001 and 2011, Jaipur district’s population grew by 26.91%, indicating a high decadal growth rate.
The district’s sex ratio in 2011 was 909 females per 1,000 males.
The literacy rate in Jaipur district was reported as 76.44% in the 2011 Census.
Urban residents comprised 52.40% of the district’s population in 2011, reflecting a slight majority living in urban areas.
Scheduled Castes accounted for 15.14% and Scheduled Tribes for 7.97% of the district’s population according to the 2011 Census.

Language data from the 2011 Census show that 45.85% of residents listed Hindi as their first language, 34.44% Rajasthani, 11.31% Dhundari, 2.74% Urdu, 2.52% Marwari, 1.21% Sindhi, 0.42% Punjabi and 0.41% Bengali.
The district is administratively divided into 13 sub‑divisions, 16 tehsils (after the addition of three new tehsils), and 13 Panchayat Samitis.

The three newly added tehsils increased the total from 13 to 16, with the current list including Amber, Bassi, Chaksu, Chomu, Dudu, Jamwa Ramgarh, Phagi, Sambhar, Jaipur, Kotputli, Shahpura, Sanganer, Viratnagar, Kot Khawada, Kishangarh‑Renwal, Mauzamabad and Paota.

title: [PDF] COMPREHENSIVE MOBILITY PLAN FOR JAIPUR
insights: The Jaipur Comprehensive Mobility Plan (CMP) combines aggressive public‑transport expansion with land‑use integration to address rapid population and business growth projected to 2025. By dramatically increasing bus, BRT, metro and monorail capacity, the plan seeks to lift public‑transport mode share from under 20% today to 50% while also improving network speeds and safety outcomes. These targets are supported by detailed investment phasing and corridor‑specific ridership forecasts, providing a data‑driven roadmap for sustainable urban mobility.
key_facts: The Master Development Plan 2011 for Jaipur, prepared by the Jaipur Development Authority, outlines a Comprehensive Mobility Plan (CMP) that targets the horizon year 2025 to meet mobility concerns arising from population and business growth in the study area.
The CMP document states that the existing bus fleet in Jaipur consists of 1,440 buses.
The plan proposes a bus fleet augmentation of 2,600 additional buses, with phased investment of Rs 0.4 crore in 2010‑2015, Rs 1,040 crore in 2015‑2020, and Rs 300‑430 crore in subsequent phases.
Metro rail investment is outlined as Rs 28 crore for 2010‑2015, Rs 250 crore for 2015‑2020, and Rs 7,000 crore for the period beyond 2020, according to the CMP.
BRT (Bus Rapid Transit) investment is detailed as Rs 100 crore for 2010‑2015, Rs 12 crore for 2015‑2020, and Rs 1,200‑450 crore for later phases.
The document lists a tourist monorail corridor with a unit cost of Rs 11 crore and a total projected investment of Rs 90 crore.
Non‑motorised transport provisions in the plan include 160 km of dedicated bike lanes and 200 km of footpaths with integrated drainage.
Mode‑share data for 2009 (peak‑hour motorised trips) show two‑wheelers at 33%, cars at 10%, auto‑rickshaws at 7%, taxis at 9%, and public transport at 10% of trips.
In the "Do Nothing" 2031 scenario, the same document reports two‑wheelers at 27%, cars at 8%, auto‑rickshaws at 6%, taxis at 9%, and public transport at 19% of trips.
Under the "With Mass Transit System" 2031 scenario, public‑transport mode share is projected to rise to approximately 23% of all trips.
Average network speed is projected to increase from 14 km/h in 2009 to 28 km/h in the 2031 "Do Nothing" scenario and further to 32 km/h in the 2031 "With Mass Transit System" scenario.
Average trip length is expected to grow from 7.9 km in 2009 to 9.5 km in the 2031 "With Mass Transit System" scenario.

Passenger‑kilometres are reported as 52.3 lakh km in 2009 and decline to 15.34 lakh km in the 2031 "Do Nothing" scenario, highlighting the impact of reduced travel demand without new transit investments.

The CMP identifies several proposed BRT corridors, including a Ring Road BRT from Ambabari to Sindhi Camp (estimated 4,200 trips), Dhani Govindapura to Ambabari (4,100 trips), Ambabari to Kanakpura Railway Station via Ajmeer Road (3,800 trips), and others totaling multiple corridors across the city.
The plan sets a target to increase public‑transport share from the present 19% to 50% by the horizon year, as part of its broader mobility objectives.
Fatalities per lakh population are targeted to be reduced from 71 (current) to 10 by the plan’s end, reflecting a strong road‑safety focus.
Walkability is targeted to improve from a current footpath‑to‑road length ratio of 51% to 100% of road length, indicating a goal of full pedestrian infrastructure coverage.
Bus occupancy is reported at 45 passengers per bus, with a maximum observed passenger volume of 3,662 passengers at Chandpole Bazaar during peak hours.
Accident statistics in the document show non‑fatal accidents peaked at 2,124 in 2006, while fatalities peaked at 454 in the same year, with varying annual growth rates thereafter.

title: [PDF] COMPREHENSIVE MOBILITY PLAN FOR JAIPUR CITY
insights: The February 2026 Jaipur Development Authority Comprehensive Mobility Plan documents a sharp rise in vehicle registrations and a transport system heavily reliant on privately operated minibuses and para‑transit, underscoring urgent needs for regulated services, congestion mitigation, and multimodal infrastructure. The plan’s extensive analysis of corridors, proposed MRTS and bus routes, and identified travel‑speed and accident trends provide a data‑driven foundation for prioritising investments that can improve accessibility, reduce emissions, and support the city’s growing economic and educational hubs.
key_facts: The Jaipur Development Authority Comprehensive Mobility Plan (draft, February 2026) reports that two‑wheel vehicle registrations rose from 2,079,028 in 2020‑21 to 2,692,163 in 2025‑26, indicating explosive growth over five years.
E‑rickshaw registrations increased from 19,477 in 2020‑21 to 33,037 in 2025‑26, reflecting expanding use of electric micro‑mobility within the city.
The plan notes that privately operated minibuses serve underserved and peripheral areas of Jaipur, functioning as supplementary modes to the formal JCTSL bus system.
Shared autos and tempos are described as a vital para‑transit layer that provides last‑mile connectivity and short‑distance travel in dense residential, market, and institutional zones.
These para‑transit services are typically privately operated, unregulated or semi‑regulated, and operate along informal yet consistent corridors throughout Jaipur.

The document identifies increased travel demand combined with limited urban transport facilities as drivers of congestion, travel delays, loss of productivity, excessive fuel consumption, deteriorating air quality, noise pollution, and a rise in road accidents and fatalities.
Inadequate transport systems are said to limit accessibility to employment, services, education, and other opportunities, contributing to social exclusion in Jaipur.

The plan cites Jaipur’s major economic generators—gemstone cutting, jewellery manufacturing, textiles, information technology, tourism, and a growing educational sector with universities such as Manipal, Amity, BITS‑Mesra, Poornima, JECRC, and LNM Institute of Information Technology.
Per Ministry of Housing & Urban Affairs (MoHUA) Guidelines 2017, a Comprehensive Mobility Plan must be revised at least once every five years; this 2026 draft fulfills that requirement.
RITES Ltd. has been engaged by the Jaipur Development Authority to prepare the Comprehensive Mobility Plan, indicating a professional consultancy involvement.
Table 2.92 in the report analyses public transport facilities, while Table 2.93 and Table 2.94 assess pedestrian and non‑motorized transport infrastructure respectively.
Table 2.95 evaluates the level of usage of Intelligent Transport Systems (ITS) across the city, and Table 2.96 examines travel speeds for motorized and mass‑transit modes along major corridors.
Figure 4.1 proposes new Mass Rapid Transit System (MRTS) corridors for Jaipur, signaling a planned expansion of high‑capacity rail transit.
Figure 4.2 and Figure 4.3 outline proposed standard bus routes and midi‑bus routes, respectively, indicating a restructuring of bus services to improve coverage.
Figure 4.4 presents proposed intercity bus terminals and depots, reflecting plans to enhance regional connectivity beyond the metropolitan area.

title: [PDF] Assessment of Urban Mobility in Jaipur using the Sustainable Urban ...
insights: The document reveals that Jaipur’s rapid vehicle growth and dominant two‑wheeler usage are driving high trip volumes and low public‑transport modal share, which together depress its Sustainable Urban Transport Index score. Planners must address the imbalance between private motorised trips and under‑utilised metro and bus services, while leveraging the sizable non‑motorised share to improve congestion and emissions.
key_facts: Jaipur’s 2011 census recorded a city population of 3.4 million within 467 sq km and a greater metropolitan population of 4.45 million spread over 2,940 sq km, highlighting a dense urban core.

The Jaipur Home Interview Survey (JMRC, 2018) estimated that 3.25 million trips are made daily in the city, with roughly 2.1 million of those occurring along a north‑south axis and the remainder east‑west.
Average home‑based trip length across all modes is 8.7 km, while the overall average trip length (including non‑home trips) is 9.1 km, and non‑home trips average 7.9 km.
Mode‑specific average home‑based trip lengths are: bus 11.4 km, car 12.6 km, two‑wheeler 5.8 km, auto‑rickshaw 5.4 km, bicycle 2.4 km, walk 1.8 km, and metro 6.1 km.
Citywide average travel speed is 16.5 km/h, dropping to under 10 km/h within the core city area, indicating congestion hotspots.
In 2017 two‑wheelers numbered 1,882,887 (67 % of registered vehicles) and private cars numbered 450,704 (16 % of registered vehicles), reflecting a motorised fleet heavily skewed toward two‑wheelers.
The total number of registered vehicles grew at an annual compound rate of 8.8 % since 2010, with cars increasing faster than two‑wheelers over the same period.
Jaipur Metro Rail Corporation operates ten four‑coach metro trains, each capable of carrying 1,506 passengers, yet only about 0.5 % of commuters use the metro according to the survey.

Public‑transport modal share shows two‑wheelers at 27 %, cars at 17 %, city buses at 18 %, and metro at 0.5 % of commuters, while non‑motorised transport (walk and cycle) accounts for 32 % (walk 26 %, cycle 6 %).
When non‑motorised modes are excluded, motorised commuting shares shift to two‑wheelers 40 %, cars 24 %, and city buses 26 % of trips.
Two‑wheelers constitute 31.7 % of total trips, making them the predominant mode despite their relatively low average trip length.
Jaipur has 143 city‑bus stops covering 262.6 sq km and serving 1,650,685 residents, roughly 54 % of the city’s population, indicating limited bus stop density.

The Sustainable Urban Transport Index (SUTI) for Jaipur scores 41.45 overall, with particularly low normalized scores for public‑transport quality and reliability (23.86), investment in public transport (11.67), and traffic fatalities (29.37).
Indicator 6 (affordability) scores 99.92 % normalized, reflecting low travel‑cost burden, while greenhouse‑gas emissions per capita score 71.95 % normalized.
Fare‑box recovery is low for city buses (25 % of operating costs covered by fares) but higher for the metro (70 % covered), illustrating differing financial sustainability between modes.

title: [PDF] Traffic and Transportation Study For DPR For Proposed Jaipur Metro ...
insights: The document shows that Jaipur is undergoing rapid demographic and vehicular expansion, with a 4.4% annual population growth and vehicle registrations rising from 100,000 in 1982 to 1.3 million by 2007. This surge, combined with a dominant two‑wheeler mode share and minimal public‑transport usage, is creating severe core‑area congestion, underscoring the urgency for high‑capacity mass‑transit solutions such as the proposed metro and ring‑road projects.
key_facts: The Jaipur Development Authority’s jurisdiction covers 474 sq km and currently houses about 3.2 million residents, a figure projected to rise to 8.1 million within the next two decades according to the study.
The Master Plan 2011 estimated Jaipur’s population at 4.2 million for the year 2011, indicating substantial growth since earlier estimates.
Jaipur’s annual population growth rate is reported as 4.4%, leading to an expected population of 5.4 million by 2021.
Registered vehicles in Jaipur increased from 100,000 in 1982 to 1.3 million in 2007, reflecting rapid motorisation over 25 years.

Household surveys show an average ownership of 0.75 two‑wheelers, 0.08 cars, and 0.12 bicycles per household, with two‑wheelers comprising roughly three‑quarters of all registered vehicles and cars about 16%.
The predominant travel mode in Jaipur is two‑wheelers, while the share of cars, auto‑rickshaws and public transport is low, contributing to severe congestion in the city core.
Peak‑hour traffic counts at the outer cordon reveal that Ajmer Road (Toll Plaza) carries the highest volume with 11,207 peak PCU and 116,735 daily PCU, representing 10% of total traffic.
Across the outer cordon, passenger vehicles account for 87% of inter‑city traffic during peak hours, with goods vehicles making up the remaining 13%.
Road accident records from 2004 to 2008 show a total of 2,042 accidents in 2004 rising to 2,367 in 2005 (12% increase) and then declining to 2,098 in 2008 (9% decrease).

Bus fare structures published by the Rajasthan State Road Transport Corporation range from Rs 3 for ordinary buses over 0‑2 km to Rs 16 for ordinary buses over distances above 35 km, with deluxe fares set higher at each distance band.
Equivalency factors for urban road traffic assign a factor of 2.2 to buses with up to 5% composition and 3.7 for buses exceeding 5% composition; minibuses have a factor of 1.
Jaipur’s air connectivity is highlighted by an airport located about 15 km from the city centre, offering regular flights to all major Indian cities and many second‑order cities.
The city lacks a commuter‑rail service, although it is regionally linked by rail lines to Delhi, Agra, Ahmedabad, Ujjain, and other major centres, with five principal railway stations within Jaipur.

Key planned infrastructure projects influencing urban growth include the Jaipur International Airport, industrial zones such as Sitapura and Vishwakarma, Special Economic Zones near the proposed outer ring road at Bhankrota, Vatika IT City, a Sports City on Delhi road, a Film City on the Jaipur‑Agra corridor, and the proposed Jaipur Ring Road.

The study’s data collection relied on secondary sources such as the Master Plan for Jaipur, bus operation details, intermediate public‑transport data, vehicle registration records (2004‑2008), road‑accident data (2004‑2008), the Mass Transit Railway System report, the Jaipur Urban Mass Transport Study, and a detailed design report for a Bus Rapid Transit System.

title: [PDF] ROAD TRAFFIC FLOW INTENSITY IN JAIPUR CITY - INSPIRA
insights: The paper paints Jaipur as a rapidly expanding metropolis whose vehicle fleet is growing at about 8.4 % annually, outpacing the capacity of its largely road‑centric transport system. High V/C ratios, low peak‑hour speeds and a bus fleet far below international standards signal severe congestion, while inadequate parking and a nascent metro exacerbate the problem, underscoring the urgency for integrated land‑use and multimodal planning.
key_facts: Jaipur, the capital of Rajasthan, is identified as the 10th largest city in India and one of the fastest‑growing urban centres, according to the 2020 IJARCMSS paper.
The 2011 Census recorded Jaipur’s population at approximately 3.1 million people, giving the city a population density of about 6 500 inhabitants per square kilometre.
The city’s total road network is reported to be around 1 500 km in length, of which roughly 34 % are two‑lane roads and about 52 % are four‑lane roads.
The average annual growth rate of motor vehicles in Jaipur is cited as roughly 8.4 % per year.
Cumulative vehicle registrations in Jaipur district rose from 1 176 754 in 2006‑07 to 2 423 648 by the end of 2015‑16.
Two‑wheelers and cars together account for 73.18 % and 13.76 % respectively of the total registered vehicles in Jaipur as of 2016.
The 2015‑16 vehicle‑type breakdown shows 1 773 513 two‑wheelers, 333 587 cars, 27 448 auto‑rickshaws, 6 128 tempo‑passenger, 14 611 tempo‑goods, 83 262 trucks, among others.
Public and private bus services in Jaipur operate at crush capacity, with only about 30 buses available per lakh population, well below the desirable benchmark of 50 buses per lakh.
The Jaipur Metro is described as being in a very early stage and does not yet provide adequate city‑wide connectivity.

Peak‑hour traffic volume‑to‑capacity (V/C) ratios on key roads in the historic (Walled) City exceed 0.75, with specific values of 0.75 on Surajpol‑Tripolia Bazar, 0.85 on Chandpol Road, and 0.81 on MI Road Ghat‑to‑Sanganeri Gate, indicating approaching unstable flow.
Average vehicle speed in commercial districts during peak periods is reported to be only 16 km h⁻¹.
A “do‑nothing” scenario projected by the authors forecasts that the overall network speed could fall to 14 km h⁻¹ by 2031 if no interventions are made.
The study notes that off‑street parking provision is insufficient, leading drivers to halt vehicles on carriageways and further aggravating congestion.
The main mode of transport in Jaipur is road transport, as stated in the study’s description of the city’s transport profile.
Average annual rainfall (railfall) for Jaipur is given as 26 cm.

title: Traffic Volume: Chandpole witnesses highest daily traffic volume in Jaipur with 3.3L vehicles: Report | Jaipur News - The Times of India
insights: The report highlights that Jaipur’s vehicle density (25,048 vehicles per sq km) far exceeds the state average, and specific corridors such as Chandpole experience extreme traffic volumes (3.3 lakh vehicles daily). This concentration of cars and two‑wheelers creates chronic congestion, signalling an urgent need for traffic management, demand‑management policies, and infrastructure upgrades to improve mobility and reduce pollution.
key_facts: A study titled 'Noise mapping, identification of hot spots, and mitigation plan for control of noise pollution in Jaipur' conducted by the Rajasthan State Pollution Control Board with CSIR‑Central Road Research Institute reported that Chandpole records the highest daily traffic in Jaipur with 3.3 lakh vehicles passing each day, according to a Times of India article dated July 5, 2024.
The same RSPCB report states that Jaipur’s overall vehicle density is 25,048 vehicles per square kilometre, which is well above the Rajasthan state average of 4,299 vehicles per square kilometre.

Other major traffic corridors in Jaipur also show high volumes: Apex Circle sees 2.9 lakh vehicles daily, Ramganj 2.8 lakh, Jawahar Nagar 1.8 lakh, JDA Circle 1.8 lakh, Khasa Kothi 1.8 lakh, Chomu Pulia 1.4 lakh, Shanti Nagar Circle 1.6 lakh, and both the Delhi‑Ajmer stretch near Harmada and Ajmer Gate record about 1 lakh vehicles per day.
In terms of vehicle type, Apex Circle registers the highest daily car traffic at 95,030 cars, followed by Jawahar Circle (68,154 cars), JDA Circle (65,532 cars), and Khasa Kothi (61,991 cars).
Two‑wheeler traffic is also heavy: Chandpole leads with 200,000 two‑wheelers daily, Ramganj follows with 183,283, and Apex Circle records 161,938 two‑wheelers per day.

The traffic volume survey that produced these figures was a classified traffic volume survey carried out in 2022 to assess base‑year traffic characteristics such as total daily volume, hourly variation, peak hour volumes, directional flows, and traffic composition.

title: [PDF] COMPREHENSIVE MOBILITY PLAN FOR JAIPUR CITY
insights: The February 2026 Comprehensive Mobility Plan shows Jaipur confronting rapid population growth (2.83% CAGR) and a surge in vehicle registrations, which together intensify congestion and strain existing transport services. To address these pressures, the plan adopts a long‑term, corridor‑focused strategy that expands the bus fleet by roughly 2,450 vehicles, adds dedicated bicycle lanes, skywalks, and grade‑separated pedestrian crossings, and upgrades key junctions, thereby prioritising public and non‑motorized transport while supporting the city’s tourism and economic hubs.
key_facts: The Comprehensive Mobility Plan (CMP) for Jaipur, prepared by the Jaipur Development Authority and released in February 2026, outlines a 20‑year transportation improvement strategy extending to 2031, including a Mobility Corridor Plan that prioritises passenger and vehicular throughput on identified key corridors.

The CMP’s Public Transit Improvement Plan (2011‑2031) proposes adding approximately 2,450 buses to the city fleet, restructuring bus routes, and constructing higher‑order mass‑transit corridors, with implementation divided into three phases: 2010‑2016, 2016‑2021, and 2021‑2031.

The plan recommends bicycle lanes along public‑transport corridors, a skywalk linking the Railway Station to the Sindhi Camp Bus Terminal to accommodate high pedestrian volumes, and grade‑separated pedestrian crossings at major corridors.

The Traffic Management Plan within the CMP calls for junction upgrades at ten major locations—Khasakoti, Sanganer Gate, Ghat Gate, Sodala, Dood Mandi, GPO, Transport Nagar, Lalkothi, New Sanganer Road, and Ajmeri Gate—to improve traffic flow and safety.
Over the past decade Jaipur’s population has grown at a compound annual growth rate of 2.83 % per year, according to the CMP’s demographic analysis.
During the tourist season the city receives roughly 70,000‑80,000 visitors each day, a factor highlighted in the CMP as influencing transport demand.
The CMP notes an “explosive” increase in the number of registered vehicles in Jaipur, underscoring rising motorisation pressures, though specific vehicle counts are not provided.

Population and employment projections in the CMP are based on land‑use transitions and consider base‑year 2024 data with forecasts for 2031, 2041, 2051 and 2055, with outer zones expected to grow faster than the municipal corporation area.
The CMP’s vision includes introducing electric buses, establishing city bus terminals, depots and charging stations, and promoting non‑motorized transport to curb private vehicle growth.
The CMP aligns with the 2017 MoHUA guideline that comprehensive mobility plans be revised at least every five years, prompting the current study by RITES Ltd.

title: Jaipur traffic report | TomTom Traffic Index
insights: The 2025 TomTom Traffic Index shows that Jaipur’s road network is experiencing slightly worsening congestion, with rush‑hour speeds dropping and travel times lengthening compared with 2024. The absence of highways means all trips rely on city streets, amplifying the impact of peak‑hour delays that now cost commuters an extra five days of travel time over the year. These trends highlight the urgency for capacity‑enhancing measures or demand‑management strategies to keep the city’s mobility sustainable.
key_facts: In 2025 the average distance driven in 15 minutes in Jaipur city was 5.1 km, which is 0.1 km less than in 2024.
The congestion level at 6 pm in Jaipur city in 2025 was 58.7%, essentially unchanged from 2024.
The worst travel day in 2025 was Friday, 17 October, when congestion peaked at 90% during the 6 pm period.
The average travel time for a 10 km drive in Jaipur city in 2025 was 29 minutes 16 seconds, 42 seconds longer than in 2024.
Average speed during rush hour in Jaipur city in 2025 was 17.5 km/h, 1 km/h slower than in 2024.
Time lost due to traffic in rush hour in 2025 amounted to 121 hours (5 days 1 hour), which is 8 hours 56 minutes more than in 2024.
Morning rush hour travel time for a 10 km trip in Jaipur city in 2025 was 32 minutes 15 seconds, with an average speed of 18.6 km/h (73.9% of free‑flow speed).
Evening rush hour travel time for a 10 km trip in Jaipur city in 2025 was 36 minutes 9 seconds, with an average speed of 16.6 km/h (94.9% of free‑flow speed).
The highway trip ratio in Jaipur was 0% because the city network contains no highways.
Monthly congestion levels for Jaipur city in 2025 ranged from a low of 48% in February to a high of 67% in July.
During off‑peak early‑morning hours (e.g., 2 am) a 10 km trip in Jaipur city took about 19–20 minutes, whereas during evening peak (e.g., 6 pm) it could take up to 37 minutes.
TomTom’s 2025 data for Jaipur are based on anonymized trip information covering more than 3.65 trillion km collected from drivers across the metropolitan and city areas.

title: [PDF] Current Transit Network Inventory and Characteristics of Jaipur City
insights: The paper shows that Jaipur’s public‑transport network is heavily skewed toward the city centre, delivering only about a fifth to a third of all trips while private two‑wheelers dominate travel. Rapid population growth (≈3 % per year) and falling average speeds signal rising congestion, underscoring the urgency of expanding service frequency, stop density and feeder connectivity to peripheral zones.
key_facts: Jaipur’s population was recorded at 3.046 million in the 2019 census, with an annual growth rate estimated between 2.8 % and 3.2 %.
Central zones of Jaipur have a stop density of 4‑6 stops per square kilometre, whereas peripheral zones have only 1‑2 stops per square kilometre.
Service frequencies in central areas range from 10 to 15 minutes, while peripheral areas experience headways of up to 30 minutes.
The Jaipur Metro Phase 1, operational since June 3 2015, spans 18 km with 11 stations (9.44 km/6 stations in Phase 1A and 8.56 km/5 stations in Phase 1B).
Daily ridership on the Jaipur Metro in 2023‑2024 was between 180,000 and 220,000 passengers, representing roughly 15‑18 % of all transit trips in the city.
The combined mode share of Jaipur’s Metro and City Bus network is estimated at 20‑30 % of total trips, leaving the majority of travel to private modes.
Two‑ and three‑wheelers account for 80 % of registered vehicles in Jaipur but generate only about 35 % of all trips.
Private two‑wheeler registrations are growing at an annual rate of 12 %, outpacing the expansion of public‑transit services.
Jaipur’s bus fleet consists of 400 low‑floor buses operating on 32 routes with 143 stops, serving the city for an average of 18 hours per day (05:30‑23:30).
Peak‑hour bus capacity currently handles 1.2‑1.5 million person‑trips per day, while the system was originally designed for 1.8 million trips.
High‑frequency bus corridors include Tonk Road (8‑10 min headway), Ajmer Road (10‑12 min), and Station Road (10‑15 min).
Medium‑frequency routes such as MI Road, JLN Road and SMS Road operate with 15‑20 min headways, and low‑frequency routes in peripheral areas run every 25‑40 minutes.
Average travel speeds on Jaipur’s road network fell from 25 km/h in 2010 to 18 km/h in 2020, indicating worsening congestion.
Forty percent of peripheral residential zones lack any transit stop within an 800‑metre walking distance, highlighting a major accessibility gap.
Eighty percent of Jaipur’s roads lack continuous footpaths, limiting safe pedestrian access to transit nodes.
Three of the eleven metro stations are underground; two of those lack elevators, with accessibility audits planned for 2024‑2025.
A 6.6 km Bus Rapid Transit pilot on Sikar Road was abandoned, illustrating challenges in sustaining dedicated bus lanes without strong political support.
A proposed Phase 1D extension aims to connect the metro with the Ajmer Road interchange, indicating future network expansion plans.

title: [PDF] COMPREHENSIVE MOBILITY PLAN FOR JAIPUR CITY
insights: The document outlines an ambitious expansion of Jaipur's bus network and a shift toward electric mobility, reflecting the city's long‑term vision of a safe, efficient and sustainable transport system. By integrating 150 e‑buses, adding 150 new shelters, and proposing extensive new corridors and bicycle lanes, planners aim to boost public‑transport accessibility while mitigating congestion and emissions. The detailed route lengths, depot allocations, and traffic‑volume data provide a quantitative baseline for evaluating future service performance and corridor upgrades.
key_facts: The proposed standard bus route from Jaipur Airport to Chandpole is 16.4 km long and includes 13 stops, as shown in Table 4.2 of the February 2026 report.
The second proposed standard bus route from the Airport to an unspecified destination spans 13.1 km with 11 stops, according to Table 4.2.
The third proposed standard bus route, designated Bagrana (JDA Parking), covers 22.4 km and has 17 stops, per Table 4.2.
The fourth proposed standard bus route, named Achrol, extends 30 km and includes 22 stops, as listed in Table 4.2.

The Comprehensive Mobility Plan (CMP) for Jaipur released in 2010 identified key mobility corridors (Figure 1.3) to improve passenger and vehicular throughput and overall Level of Service.

The CMP’s Public Transit Improvement Plan for 2011‑2031 proposed adding approximately 2,450 buses, restructuring routes, and developing higher‑order mass‑transit corridors, with implementation phases covering 2010‑2016, 2016‑2021 and 2021‑2031.

Jaipur City Transport Services Limited (JCTSL) has proposed operating 150 electric buses on 17 routes, with nine routes based at the Bagrana depot and eight at the Todi depot, to modernize the city bus system.
JCTSL also plans to install 150 new bus queue shelters along existing high‑demand routes to improve passenger waiting facilities, as detailed in Annexure 1.1.
Jaipur International Airport, situated in Sanganer about 13 km from the city core, handled 5.46 million passengers in the fiscal year 2024‑25.

The city’s bus transport system is described as comprehensive, with major terminals at Sindhi Camp, Narayan Singh Circle, and Vaishali Nagar, and the Rajasthan State Road Transport Corporation (RSRTC) operating a wide range of services from ordinary to Volvo buses connecting Jaipur to major regional and inter‑state destinations.
Jaipur’s existing public‑transport mix includes government‑operated JCTSL buses, privately operated minibuses, and the Jaipur Metro, indicating a multimodal network.

Traffic intensity data at the Agra‑Jaipur Road (MB‑01) show a total of 20,968 PCUs in both directions, with fast‑moving passenger vehicles accounting for 44.58% and buses for 27.27% of the traffic composition.

The CMP proposes bicycle lanes along public‑transport corridors, a skywalk linking the Railway Station with Sindhi Camp Bus Terminal, and grade‑separated pedestrian crossings at major corridors to address high pedestrian volumes.

The CMP’s Traffic Management Plan includes junction improvements at key locations such as Khasakoti, Sanganer Gate, Ghat Gate, Sodala, Dood Mandi, GPO, Transport Nagar, Lalkothi, New Sanganer Road, and Ajmeri Gate to enhance traffic flow and safety.

title: [PDF] Assessment of Urban Mobility in Jaipur using the Sustainable Urban ...
insights: The document reveals that Jaipur faces severe non‑motorised transport deficiencies, high vehicle density and rapid motorisation, all of which strain its road network and parking capacity. Planned interventions such as a comprehensive mobility corridor, outer ring road and metro expansion are critical to integrate modes and alleviate congestion, but funding gaps and weak inter‑agency coordination threaten their implementation.
key_facts: Missing footpaths are a characteristic of the majority of Jaipur's road network, and many existing footpaths are encroached by informal traders, forcing pedestrians to share space with vehicles.
Safe pedestrian crossing systems are absent on most city roads, further compromising pedestrian safety.
Bicycle lanes are virtually nonexistent in Jaipur despite a large number of cyclists using the streets.

The city plans a comprehensive mobility corridor that will integrate road, rail and non‑motorised transport, including an outer ring road and six link roads that will connect to regional and radial roads.
Jaipur had 2,791,139 registered vehicles in 2017, representing roughly 19% of all registered vehicles in the state of Rajasthan.
Vehicle density in Jaipur was 25,048 vehicles per square kilometre in 2017, about five times the state average of 4,299 vehicles per square kilometre (Bansal, 2017).
Two‑wheelers and private cars together accounted for 83% of Jaipur's registered vehicles in 2017, with two‑wheelers comprising 67% and private cars 16% of the fleet.
Parking is constrained by limited off‑street facilities and widespread free on‑street parking, which aggravates traffic management and slows vehicle movement.

Jaipur Metro Rail Corporation operates Line 1, a 12‑km east‑west corridor, and plans to start construction of Line 2, a 23‑km north‑south corridor, in 2020; the metro currently serves two routes with 11 stations.
Footpaths in Jaipur total about 210 km, roughly one‑tenth of the city's total road length, and are described as inadequate and poorly maintained (Jaipur Development Authority, 2011).
A home‑based travel survey found an average home‑based trip length of 8.7 km and a total average trip length of 9.1 km, with 3.25 million trips made daily in the city (JMRC, 2018).
The same survey reported that approximately 2.1 million of those daily trips occur along the north‑south axis, with the remainder traveling east‑west.
Average trip lengths by mode are: bus 11.4 km, car 12.6 km, two‑wheeler 5.8 km, auto‑rickshaw 5.4 km, bicycle 2.4 km, walk 1.8 km, and metro 6.1 km.
Average travel speed across Jaipur is 16.5 km/h, dropping to less than 10 km/h within the core city area.

Land‑use distribution in Jaipur shows residential use at 54.4%, commercial at 11.8%, and transport (circulation) occupying 10% of the city's area, matching the ideal transport share cited by Litman (2018).

Jaipur's road network follows a hierarchical grid‑iron pattern with ten radial and three circular roads, ten major arterial roads, and a total length of about 2,500 km (Jaipur Development Authority, 2011).
A 144‑km peripheral ring road is planned to improve connectivity between regional and radial roads.
A Bus Rapid Transit System operated on a 6.6‑km stretch between Sikar and Pani Petch but was later discontinued due to lack of state support.
Jaipur City Transport Services Limited runs a fleet of 400 low‑floor buses on 32 routes, serving 143 bus stops, complemented by roughly 55 privately operated minibuses.
Registered vehicle numbers have grown at an annual compound rate of 8.8% since 2010, with cars increasing faster than two‑wheelers.
The metro system currently uses ten four‑coach trains, each capable of carrying 1,506 passengers.
Public‑transport modal share shows two‑wheelers at 27%, cars at 17%, city buses at 18%, non‑motorised modes at 32% (walk 26%, cycle 6%), and metro usage at only about 0.5% of commuters.
Excluding non‑motorised modes, two‑wheelers account for 40% of motorised trips, cars 24%, and city buses 26% in Jaipur.
Topographical constraints in the north‑east of Jaipur limit the expansion of road connectivity, while rising per‑capita income is expected to further increase vehicle demand.
To meet the Comprehensive Mobility Plan 2018 objectives, Jaipur faces an estimated budget shortfall of approximately INR 245 billion.

title: [PDF] COMPREHENSIVE MOBILITY PLAN FOR JAIPUR CITY
insights: The Jaipur mobility documents reveal a long‑term, multi‑modal strategy that couples corridor‑level capacity upgrades with a massive public‑transit expansion and targeted traffic‑management interventions. By prioritising key radial and national‑highway corridors, completing the southern Outer Ring Road, and restricting mixed‑traffic e‑rickshaws, planners aim to separate fast and slow streams, reduce bottlenecks, and shape future urban growth along the southern periphery.
key_facts: The Comprehensive Mobility Plan (CMP) for the Jaipur Region, prepared by the Jaipur Development Authority in 2010, set a 20‑year horizon to guide transportation improvements up to 2031.

The CMP identified a set of “Key Mobility Corridors” (shown in Figure 1.3) that were prioritized for capacity augmentation and traffic‑management measures to improve passenger and vehicular throughput.

The Public Transit Improvement Plan within the CMP proposed adding approximately 2,450 buses, restructuring bus routes, and developing higher‑order mass‑transit corridors in three implementation phases (2010‑2016, 2016‑2021, 2021‑2031).

The plan recommended restricting e‑rickshaw operations on ten specific routes (illustrated in Figure 4.8) because mixed traffic with slow‑moving e‑rickshaws creates speed differentials, capacity loss, and safety conflicts.
Jaipur’s road network follows a radial‑and‑grid pattern, with major radial arterials extending from the historic walled city and linking the core to peripheral growth centres.
Two national highways traverse Jaipur: NH 48 (Delhi‑Ajmer‑Mumbai corridor) and NH 52 (Jaipur‑Kota‑Bhopal corridor), serving both regional and intra‑city traffic.

The southern alignment of the Outer Ring Road (ORR), a 47‑km stretch, has been completed and is operating as a bypass for through traffic and as a catalyst for planned urban expansion along Jaipur’s southern periphery.
The northern alignment of the ORR is shown in Figure 4.9, though its construction status is not detailed in the excerpt.

The CMP proposed bicycle lanes along public‑transport corridors, a skywalk linking the Railway Station to the Sindhi Camp Bus Terminal, and grade‑separated pedestrian crossings at major corridors to address high pedestrian volumes.

The Traffic Management Plan in the CMP called for junction improvements at ten major intersections (including Khasakoti, Sanganer Gate, Ghat Gate, Sodala, Dood Mandi, GPO, Transport Nagar, Lalkothi, New Sanganer Road, and Ajmeri Gate) along with bus shelters, better street lighting, signage, and safety measures.

The Comprehensive Traffic and Transportation Study (CTTS) for the Jaipur Region, also prepared by the Jaipur Development Authority, extends the investment horizon to 2037 and aligns with the National Urban Transport Policy of 2006.

Table 0.13 lists fifteen proposed road‑widening projects, converting two‑lane sections to four‑lane or six‑lane capacity; examples include the Rampura Dabri‑Jahota stretch (4.3 km) and the Jaisinghpura‑Bawadi stretch (10.2 km).

The CTTS includes proposed MRTS (Mass Rapid Transit System) corridors (Figure 1.6) and detailed standard‑bus, midi‑bus, and intercity‑bus routes (Tables 4.1‑4.4), indicating a multimodal expansion strategy.

The document references tables on annual registered vehicles (Table 2.6) and accident statistics (Table 2.7), implying that vehicle ownership and safety data are part of the broader analysis, though specific figures are not quoted in the excerpt.

title: Press Release:Press Information Bureau
insights: The document highlights a rapid expansion of India's highway infrastructure, with multiple high‑cost expressways and corridor projects inaugurated in early 2023 that are expected to cut travel times and stimulate regional economies. The substantial increase in National Highway length—about 60% since 2014—and the aggressive construction pace under the Bharatmala Pariyojana illustrate a strategic focus on improving freight and passenger mobility, which is critical for future transport planning and congestion management.
key_facts: On 12 February 2023, the 246‑km Delhi‑Dausa‑Lalsot section of the Delhi‑Mumbai Expressway was inaugurated, a development projected to substantially reduce travel time from the National Capital to Jaipur and to boost tourism at Sariska, Keoladeo National Park, Ranthambore and Jaipur.

During the same ceremony, a foundation stone was laid for 247 km of National Highway projects costing more than Rs 5,940 crore, including a four‑lane spur road from Bandikui to Jaipur, a six‑lane spur road from Kotputli to Baraodaneo, and a two‑lane paved shoulder on the Lalsot‑Karoli section.

On 12 March 2023, the 118‑km Bengaluru‑Mysuru Expressway was dedicated at a cost of Rs 8,480 crore, a route that will cut travel time between Bengaluru and Mysuru from three hours to about 75 minutes and is expected to spur socio‑economic development in the region.

On the same day, a foundation stone was laid for the 92‑km Mysuru‑Kushalnagar four‑lane highway in Mandya, Karnataka, with an estimated cost of Rs 4,130 crore, intended to improve connectivity between Bengaluru and Kushalnagar.

India’s total road network totals approximately 66.71 lakh km, making it the second‑largest in the world, with National Highways accounting for 1,46,145 km, State Highways 1,79,535 km, and other roads 63,45,403 km.
The National Highway network grew from 91,287 km in 2014 to 1,46,145 km in 2023, representing an increase of roughly 60 percent over nine years.
The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) has constructed a provisional total of 5,248 km of National Highways between 2014‑15 and 2023‑24.
Annual NH construction peaked at 13,327 km in 2020‑21, averaging 36.5 km per day, demonstrating an accelerating pace of highway development.

The Bharatmala Pariyojana, launched in October 2017, targets the development of 34,800 km of National Highways under Phase I, focusing on economic corridors, inter‑corridor and feeder routes, and expressways to improve goods and passenger movement.

On 7 July 2023, five National Highway projects worth Rs 6,400 crore were launched in Raipur, including a 33‑km four‑lane stretch from Raipur to Kodebod, a 53‑km four‑lane Bilaspur‑Pathrapali segment, a 43‑km six‑lane Jhanki‑Sargi section, a 57‑km six‑lane Sargi‑Basanwahi stretch, and a 25‑km six‑lane Basanwahi‑Marangpuri link, all aimed at enhancing regional connectivity and socio‑economic development.

On 8 July 2023, a 176‑km National Highway initiative valued at Rs 5,500 crore was inaugurated in Warangal, featuring a 108‑km Mancherial‑Warangal segment of the Nagpur‑Vijayawada Corridor and the upgradation of a 68‑km Karimnagar‑Warangal stretch of NH‑563 from two‑lane to four‑lane configuration.

title: [PDF] indicators to measure performance efficiency of bus systems
insights: The document compares urban and rural bus system utilization among Indian state transport undertakings, revealing that BMTC and Karnataka SRTC achieve higher station and fleet utilization than their counterparts DTC and OSRTC. It also highlights methodological inconsistencies in occupancy and load‑factor calculations and stresses the need for demand‑driven scheduling, infrastructure investment, and cost‑efficiency to balance mobility and financial sustainability.
key_facts: The urban system utilization indicator shows that BMTC’s station utilization is higher than that of Delhi Transport Corporation (DTC), indicating greater passenger traffic per station for BMTC.
In the rural system utilization indicator, Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation (Karnataka SRTC) exhibits higher station utilization than Odisha State Road Transport Corporation (OSRTC).

Annual ridership per bus, which normalizes ridership by the total number of buses held by the SRTU (including off‑road buses), is significantly higher for BMTC and Karnataka SRTC than for DTC and OSRTC respectively.

The document notes that an extensive, high‑frequency bus network offered at affordable prices—often cheaper than the marginal cost of a two‑wheeler—can attract many commuters but may create oversupply and large gaps between system cost and revenue.
In some small cities, bus service consists of a single route across the city, with intercity SRTU buses used for city operations and scheduling not based on demand analysis.
The second level of bus services includes more than one route, with scheduling based on observed higher demand during morning and evening peaks.
Metropolitan cities such as Bangalore, Delhi, Mumbai, and Pune have publicly owned transport companies whose services are based on demand analysis.
Improvements in reliability, speed, availability, and cost reduction can be achieved through better scheduling, feeder systems, road‑design changes, bus‑stop placement, and signal‑system upgrades.
The bus system is capable of carrying 100 persons per bus to about 40,000 persons per hour, depending on the design strategies employed.

Public‑transport policies must balance conflicting goals such as mobility for all and safety for all, requiring data‑driven results for operations management, transport planning, policy‑making, or strategic decision‑making.

Occupancy ratio is based on seats available, while load factor is based on total carrying capacity (seats plus standing spaces); for some SRTUs (APSRTC, MSRTC, UPSRTC) the figures are identical, whereas for others (BMTC, KDTC, BEST) they differ, suggesting possible miscalculation by applying the same formula to both indicators (CIRT 2012‑13).

In the urban case study, DTC has higher utilization (passenger‑km per vehicle‑km) than BMTC, interpreted as a higher average number of passengers per bus at any given time; typical metropolitan bus operations values range from 45 to 54 passenger‑km per vehicle‑km.
In rural operations, the utilization range can be wider on both ends, as shown in the rural system utilization figure.
The document lists trip‑cost values of 1,551.66 ₹, 606.48 ₹, 1,398.57 ₹ and 11,763.63 ₹ per trip, noting that lower values indicate better cost efficiency.
Operating cost is defined as total cost minus total interest and total tax.
The cost calculations apply only to SRTU‑owned buses and do not include hired buses.

title: [PDF] Women's safety in Public Transportation: A case study of Jaipur city ...
insights: The document reveals that despite a high proportion of educated, licensed women in Jaipur, public buses remain the primary mode for daily travel due to congestion, cost, and limited metro coverage, yet safety concerns are pronounced and undermine satisfaction. Addressing infrastructure, boarding/alighting safety, and information access could improve female commuters' perception and increase their share of sustainable public transport, which is critical for supporting the city’s growing female workforce and mitigating traffic congestion.
key_facts: Jaipur, the largest city in Rajasthan and known as the "Pink City," had an approximate population of 3.073 million according to the 2011 census, with the majority classified as urban residents.
The city is situated amidst the Aravalli hills in a semi‑arid climate characterized by high summer temperatures, limited rainfall, and mild winters.
Jaipur serves as a commercial hub for the state, a role that contributes to significant traffic congestion and rapid urbanization.
Good road and air connectivity links Jaipur with major Indian cities, supporting its status as a metropolitan centre.
A questionnaire administered to female commuters yielded 439 valid responses for analysis of safety perceptions on public buses.
Among the respondents, 38.95% are students who rely on public buses to reach educational institutions, while 23.91% are working women employed in government or private sectors.
The study found that 58.77% of female respondents hold a driving licence yet continue to use public buses because of high urban congestion and the expense of private vehicle travel.
Eighty point five nine percent of the surveyed women fall in the 18‑25 age bracket and 13.73% are aged 26‑40, indicating a predominantly youthful commuter base.
Only 4.55% of the women surveyed were reported as illiterate, suggesting that the majority are educated and capable of contributing to the economy.
Vehicle ownership among respondents is low: 5.69% own a four‑wheeler, while 62.65% of households own one or more two‑wheelers.
Household two‑wheelers distribution shows 5.69% with none, 43.96% with one, 40.77% with two, and 9.56% with more than two two‑wheelers.
Household four‑wheelers distribution shows 37.35% with none, 48.06% with one, 11.61% with two, and 2.96% with more than two four‑wheelers.
Public‑bus usage frequency among female commuters is 18.45% daily, 52.84% occasional, 17.31% once in a while, and 11.38% rarely.
Satisfaction scores for public‑bus attributes on a 1‑5 scale indicate the highest satisfaction for cost (average 3.054) and the lowest for safety (average 2.293).

Factor analysis identified four major determinants of perceived safety on buses: infrastructure and operations, boarding/alighting concerns, information accessibility, and positive sentiments toward bus stops.
Although Jaipur has metro facilities, their limited coverage on key routes makes public buses the preferred choice for female commuters.
The study emphasizes that improving lighting, level surfaces, and overall bus‑stop design could enhance safety for women and encourage greater public‑transport mode share.

These conditions underscore the need for coordinated route planning, service reliability improvements, and substantial investment to meet the Comprehensive Mobility Plan targets.

Within a 500‑metre buffer around bus stops, the average population density is 262.6 inhabitants per hectare, covering 1,628,685.2 inhabitants.
60.96% of Jaipur’s population lives within 500 m of a bus stop, indicating moderate spatial accessibility to bus services.

A total of 3.25 million trips are made daily in Jaipur, with about 2.1 million of those occurring along the north‑south corridor and the remainder along the east‑west corridor.
Average monthly transport cost for commuters using city buses and the metro represents about 3.53% of household income, yielding a high affordability normalized score of 99.92.

The Comprehensive Mobility Plan (CMP) 2018 identifies a budgetary shortfall of roughly INR 245 billion needed to achieve its transport investment objectives, casting doubt on the implementation of planned projects.

insights: The document shows that Jaipur's metropolitan area is projected to more than double its 2011 population by 2055, while decadal growth rates are slowing, underscoring the urgency for a phased, multimodal transport strategy that can accommodate rising demand without exacerbating congestion. By linking demographic forecasts with detailed mobility corridor, public‑transit, and traffic‑management plans, the study provides a data‑driven foundation for coordinated institutional mechanisms and investment prioritisation across buses, electric fleets, non‑motorized infrastructure, and intelligent transport systems.
key_facts: The Jaipur Development Authority (JDA) study area covers 2,940 square kilometres and comprises the Jaipur Municipal Corporation, 15 satellite towns and 725 villages, as defined in the Jaipur Master Plan‑2025.
According to the 2011 Census of India, the JDA area had a population of 4,050,087 residents.
Population grew from 2,068,180 in 1991 to 3,087,933 in 2001, reflecting a 49.3% decadal increase, but the growth slowed to 31.2% between 2001 and 2011 when the population reached 4,050,047.
Since 1991, roughly one million (10 lakh) people have been added to the study area each decade, indicating a sustained absolute increase despite the declining percentage growth.

Population is projected to reach 5.586 million (55.86 lakh) by 2024 with an annual growth rate of 2.6%, 6.642 million (66.42 lakh) by 2031 at 2.5% p.a., 8.315 million (83.15 lakh) by 2041 at 2.3% p.a., 9.576 million (95.76 lakh) by 2051 at 1.4% p.a., and 10.13 million (101.3 lakh) by 2055 at 1.4% p.a.

The 2055 forecast incorporates assumptions about development plans, existing and proposed land‑use, past growth trends (including CTTS Jaipur 2022), major transport infrastructure projects, socio‑economic trends, and high‑density transit‑oriented development along key corridors.

The Comprehensive Mobility Plan (CMP) for Jaipur, prepared by the JDA, targets a 20‑year horizon and outlines an investment programme up to 2031, featuring a Mobility Corridor Plan that prioritises passenger and vehicular throughput on identified corridors.

The CMP’s Public Transit Improvement Plan proposes adding approximately 2,450 buses, restructuring bus routes, and developing higher‑order mass‑transit corridors, with implementation phased for 2010‑2016, 2016‑2021 and 2021‑2031.

Bicycle lanes were recommended along public‑transport corridors, a skywalk between the Railway Station and Sindhi Camp Bus Terminal was proposed to serve high pedestrian volumes, and grade‑separated pedestrian crossings were suggested at major corridors.

The CMP’s Traffic Management Plan calls for junction upgrades at ten key locations, including Khasakoti, Sanganer Gate, Ghat Gate, Sodala, Dood Mandi, GPO, Transport Nagar, Lalkothi, New Sanganer Road, and Ajmeri Gate, to improve flow and safety.
MoHUA Guidelines (2017) require that a Comprehensive Mobility Plan be revised at least every five years, prompting the JDA to engage RITES Ltd. for the current mobility study.

The vision of the new CMP is to achieve safe, efficient, reliable and seamless mobility in Jaipur, with objectives that include promoting city bus services, introducing electric buses, supporting City Transport SPVs, and building infrastructure such as bus terminals, depots and charging stations.

The plan emphasizes the use of advanced urban transport planning models (CUBE/VISUM) and cost‑benefit analysis to evaluate current strategies and alternative scenarios, aligning with the National Urban Transport Policy to prioritize public and non‑motorized transport over private vehicle growth.

The Comprehensive Traffic and Transportation Study (CTTS) for Jaipur (2022) notes that outer zones of the study area are expected to grow faster than the municipal corporation, implying future shifts in travel demand and the need for corridor‑focused interventions.

title: Bikes on Rent in Jaipur with Zero Deposit at ₹ 8/Hour
insights: The document reveals a rapidly expanding two‑wheel mobility ecosystem in Jaipur, with extensive station coverage, ultra‑low hourly pricing and strong usage metrics that suggest high demand for flexible, low‑cost travel. For transport planners, such a digital bike‑sharing service can alleviate congestion, reduce private car reliance and complement public transit, especially given its reach into key commercial, academic and residential zones and its appeal to both residents and tourists.
key_facts: ONN Bikes operates bike‑rental stations in Jaipur at key locations such as C‑Scheme, Vaishali Nagar, MI Road, Bapu Bazaar, Malviya Nagar, Mansarovar and Amer Road, providing city‑wide coverage for commuters and tourists.
The service reports more than 200,000 riders have used the platform, indicating substantial user adoption in Jaipur.
The ONN Bikes app has been downloaded over one million times, reflecting broad awareness and digital engagement.
The fleet listed on the platform comprises over five thousand two‑wheelers, including scooters, commuter bikes, sports bikes and cruisers.
Over two million rides have been completed through the ONN Bikes network, demonstrating high utilization of the rental service.
ONN Bikes operates in more than twenty Indian cities, showing the scalability of its model beyond Jaipur.
Hourly rentals are priced at ₹8 per hour with zero deposit, offering an ultra‑low‑cost option for short trips.
Daily rentals start at ₹119 per day, and monthly subscription plans are marketed as comparable to EMI payments, providing flexible pricing for longer‑term users.
The company provides helmets, roadside assistance and doorstep delivery as part of its rental package, enhancing safety and convenience.
The digital onboarding process requires only a driving licence and government‑issued ID, enabling fully online verification and instant booking.
Sambhar Lake, located about 80 km from Jaipur, covers roughly 230 sq km and is promoted as a one‑day bike‑tour destination.
The Chand Baori stepwell at Abhaneri, about 95 km from Jaipur, descends 30 m and is highlighted as a nearby heritage site.
Neemrana Fort Palace, a 15th‑century fort turned heritage hotel, lies approximately 122 km from Jaipur and is featured for day trips.
Bhangarh Fort, a 16th‑century ruin, is situated roughly 83 km from Jaipur and is promoted for weekend rides.
The service emphasizes “zero hidden fees” and transparent pricing, positioning itself as an affordable alternative to private vehicle ownership.

title: [PDF] COMPREHENSIVE MOBILITY PLAN FOR JAIPUR CITY
insights: The draft Comprehensive Mobility Plan (CMP) for Jaipur, released in February 2026, outlines an extensive suite of infrastructure and policy interventions aimed at accommodating rapid urban expansion and rising travel demand through 2055. By integrating new MRTS corridors, bus networks, non‑motorized facilities, and targeted traffic‑management measures, the plan seeks to shift travel toward public and active modes while mitigating congestion and safety risks associated with explosive vehicle growth.
key_facts: The CMP 2026 proposes a network of MRTS corridors in Jaipur, as illustrated in Figure 4.1 of the report.
Standard bus routes and midi‑bus routes are planned for Jaipur, detailed in Figures 4.2 and 4.3 respectively.
Intercity bus terminals and depots are included in the proposed transport infrastructure, shown in Figure 4.4.
Bicycle lanes are proposed to run alongside public‑transport corridors to promote non‑motorized travel.
A skywalk linking the Railway Station and Sindhi Camp Bus Terminal is proposed to accommodate high pedestrian volumes.
Grade‑separated pedestrian crossings are planned at major corridors and pedestrian‑intensive locations to improve safety.

The Traffic Management Plan within the CMP calls for junction improvements, bus shelters, enhanced street lighting, road signage, and safety measures at ten major junctions including Khasakoti, Sanganer Gate, Ghat Gate, Sodala, Dood Mandi, GPO, Transport Nagar, Lalkothi, New Sanganer Road, and Ajmeri Gate.

The Comprehensive Traffic and Transportation Study (CTTS) prepared by the Jaipur Development Authority aims to define a long‑term transportation strategy and investment program up to 2037, aligning with the National Urban Transport Policy (NUTP) of 2006.
Population and employment projections for the study area consider base year 2024 and horizon years 2031, 2041, 2051, and 2055, using Census 2011, Master Plan, and CTTS 2022 data.

The demographic projection notes that towns surrounding Jaipur are expected to experience rapid population growth driven by industrial and commercial development, leading to increased traffic interactions with the city.
The outer zones of Jaipur are projected to grow faster than the Municipal Corporation area due to urban expansion.

The CMP vision emphasizes safe, efficient, reliable, and seamless mobility, with objectives that include promoting city bus services, introducing electric buses, and establishing bus terminals, depots, and charging stations.
MoHUA Guidelines (2017) require the CMP to be revised at least every five years; the current draft reflects the latest revision cycle.
